newsitem.title: UK: Calls for reform of UK utility regulators grow.
newsitem.headline: Calls for reform of UK utility regulators grow.

text.p: Calls for reform of Britain's privatised utility regulators gathered momentum on Tuesday after a report by an independent commission highlighted complaints about rulings made by the watchdogs.
The Confederation of British Industry (CBI) welcomed the report's recommendations that duties of the regulators should be clarified and advisory boards for regulators set up.

The report from the independent Commission on the Regulation of Privatised Utilities had highlighted complaints over "a lack of clarity and transparency concerning the arguments and justification" underlying regulatory decisions.
Opposition Labour party energy spokesman John Battle said the report showed that there was "an increasing consensus that there is a need to reform the system of utility regulation".
His comments and those of the CBI were echoed by Electricity Association president David Jefferies in the group's annual review, which was also published on Tuesday.
Jefferies said that "greater accountability and transparency is desirable" from the regulator.

The Commission, which is backed by an education charity, the Hansard Society, and independent think-tank the European Policy Forum, suggested that advisory boards would "increase the transparency, effectiveness and legitimacy" of regulation.
Heads of regulatory bodies should have to give reasons for their decisions and should publish an account of their guiding principles, it said.
The Commission rejected the idea of a single regulatory body to cover all utilities, which the CBI said it supported.
But it did suggest that electricity regulators Offer and Ofgas, which watches over the gas industry, could be merged after full competition in the two areas was established in 1998.
The Commission was launched in October 1995 and considered regulation in the electricity, water, gas and telecommunications industries.
It is independent and not affiliated to any political party, and there is no obligation for its recommendations to be followed by the government.
The report called on the government to publish an "explicit framework" for utilities to meet "social objectives such as universal service or energy conservation".
It said competition policy should be strengthened with enforcement by the industry regulators with the role of ministers in takeovers and mergers diminishing.
The Commission took written evidence from around 70 bodies including the regulators themselves.
